title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 230 (Power to compromise or make arrangements with creditors and members)

content.overview: Section 230 allows the Tribunal to order a meeting of creditors or members, and to sanction a compromise or arrangement if the statutory majority and fairness conditions are met.
content.glance: Section 230 allows the Tribunal to order a meeting of creditors or members, and to sanction a compromise or arrangement if the statutory majority and fairness conditions are met.
content.study: An application may be made by the company, a creditor, a member, or in liquidation the liquidator. The Tribunal may order a meeting. The notice must disclose the effect on creditors, members, promoters and directors, and any material interest. The majority required is a majority of persons representing three-fourths in value of the creditors or members voting. An objection may be made by persons holding not less than 5 per cent of the shareholding or 5 per cent of the outstanding debt. The order may provide for buy-back, takeover, or debt restructuring within the section. A take-over offer under the section has additional conditions. The order binds once filed. Listed companies also face SEBI and stock-exchange conditions; those are additional, not a replacement of s. 230.

examples.title: Value test
examples.body: A headcount majority without the three-fourths value is not enough.

examples.title: Buy-back in a scheme
examples.body: A scheme may include a buy-back element, but s. 68 conditions are not thereby ignored unless the order structures them.

distinctions: Section 230 is compromise or arrangement. Section 232 is a merger or amalgamation scheme. Oppression relief is ss 241-242 and is not a substitute scheme.

misconceptions.correction: Section 230 allows the Tribunal to order a meeting of creditors or members, and to sanction a compromise or arrangement if the statutory majority and fairness conditions are met.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Is a simple majority enough to approve a scheme?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: No. The statute requires a majority of persons representing three-fourths in value of those voting.
